backfill_note: The experiment ran on 2026-06-19 on a single Windows node; the downloaded nats-server / nats CLI binaries and the temporary JetStream store were deleted after the run per the finite-disk policy (received_images: none — no Docker was used). No hashes were captured at the time (this predates packaging). run.sh + fixture/schedule-cases.tsv are reconstructed from the run's recorded methodology so a third party can reproduce the METHOD against the same pinned versions. Unlike a live-DB benchmark, the findings here are deterministic protocol behaviors, so re-running with nats-server 2.14.2 + nats CLI 0.4.0 should reproduce them.

environment.os: Windows 11 x64, single node (native, no Docker/WSL)
environment.note: This is a scheduler protocol-behavior and syntax-acceptance check, plus a small timing observation (inter-arrival drift). It is NOT a throughput benchmark; CPU/RAM do not change the accept/reject or durability outcomes.

subject.name: nats-server
subject.note: JetStream API Level 4. Server started with: nats-server.exe -js -sd <store> -p 4222 -m 8222. Message-scheduler streams are created with --allow-schedules.

data_source.name: none (local single node)
data_source.note: No external live database. All outcomes are produced by the local nats-server under test; nothing drifts between runs given the same pinned versions.

raw_artifacts.retention_policy: discarded at run time (finite local disk)
raw_artifacts.note: Binaries + JetStream store deleted after the run. No hashes were captured at the time. Reconstructed harness (run.sh + fixture) is committed instead; that is stated plainly rather than fabricating hashes. results.json holds the behaviors and the one timing figure observed on 2026-06-19.
